text: The successive 5 ionisation energies of an element are $800,2427,3658,25024$ and $32824\mathrm{kJ}/\mathrm{mol}$, respectively. By using the above values predict the group in which the above element is present :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
We can determine the number of valence electrons by looking for a large jump in successive ionization energies. Here's how we can analyze the data:

The ionization energies given are:

$IE_{1}=800\text{kJ/mol}$ 

$IE_{2}=2427\text{kJ/mol}$ 

$IE_{3}=3658\text{kJ/mol}$ 

$IE_{4}=25024\text{kJ/mol}$ 

$IE_{5}=32824\text{kJ/mol}$

Notice that:

The first three ionization energies are relatively low.

There is a significant jump between the third and fourth ionization energy. 

What does the gap indicate?

The large jump from $IE_{3}$ to $IE_{4}$ means that after removing the first three electrons (which are the valence electrons), the next electron to be removed (a core electron) is much more strongly bound.

This implies that the element has 3 valence electrons.

Which group does an element with 3 valence electrons belong to?

Elements with 3 valence electrons are found in Group 13 of the periodic table.

Thus, the element most likely belongs to Group 13.

Correct Answer: Option C (Group 13).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{S}(\mathrm{g})+\dfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\to \mathrm{SO}_{3}(\mathrm{g})+2x\mathrm{kcal} \\ \mathrm{SO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\to \mathrm{SO}_{3}(\mathrm{g})+y\mathrm{kcal} \end{array}$

The heat of formation of $\mathrm{SO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$ is given by :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the heat of formation for $\mathrm{SO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$, we need to consider the given reactions and their enthalpy changes.

The reactions are:

$\mathrm{S}(\mathrm{g})+\frac{3}{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\to \mathrm{SO}_{3}(\mathrm{g})+2x\mathrm{kcal}$

$\mathrm{SO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}(\mathrm{g})\to \mathrm{SO}_{3}(\mathrm{g})+y\mathrm{kcal}$

For reaction 2, we have:

$\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{r}}=(\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{f}})_{\mathrm{SO}_{3}}-(\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{f}})_{\mathrm{SO}_{2}}=-y$

Given that:

$-\mathrm{y}=-2\mathrm{x}-(\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{f}})_{\mathrm{SO}_{2}}$

Rearranging this equation gives:

$(\Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{f}})_{\mathrm{SO}_{2}}=y-2x$

Thus, the heat of formation for $\mathrm{SO}_{2}(\mathrm{g})$ is $y-2x$ kcal.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift

solution.body:
Silver cyanide is largely covalent, so only the lone pair on nitrogen is available for attack, and an alkyl halide gives the isocyanide:

$\mathrm{R}-\mathrm{Cl}+\mathrm{AgCN}\longrightarrow \mathrm{R}-\mathrm{NC}+\mathrm{AgCl}$

The only $sp^{3}$ carbon-halogen bond in the substrate is the benzylic $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Cl}$ of the $-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{Cl}$ group, which is replaced to give $-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{NC}$.

The $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{I}$ and $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Br}$ bonds are on the benzene ring, where the $sp^{2}$ carbon and partial double-bond character from resonance make aryl halides inert to nucleophilic substitution; iodine stays on the ring even though $\mathrm{I}{}^{-}$ is the better leaving group in alkyl halides.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
Based on the data given below :

$\begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}/\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}}^{\circ }=1.33\mathrm{V} & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cl}_{2}/\mathrm{Cl}^{(-)}}^{\circ }=1.36\mathrm{V} \\ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}}^{0}=1.51\mathrm{V} & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}/\mathrm{Cr}}^{\circ }=-0.74\mathrm{V} \end{array}$

the strongest reducing agent is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the strongest reducing agent among the options, we need to consider which species most readily donates electrons (i.e., is most easily oxidized). One standard method is to compare the standard reduction potentials of the corresponding half-reactions. A lower (more negative) standard reduction potential indicates that the reduced species is less stable and more prone to oxidation.

Here’s the data provided:

$\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}+14H^{+}+6e^{-}\to 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}+7H_{2}O,E^{\circ }=+1.33V$  

$\mathrm{Cl}_{2}+2e^{-}\to 2\mathrm{Cl}^{-},E^{\circ }=+1.36V$  

$\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}+8H^{+}+5e^{-}\to \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+4H_{2}O,E^{\circ }=+1.51V$  

$\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}+3e^{-}\to \mathrm{Cr},E^{\circ }=-0.74V$  

Now, let’s consider the species from the Options:

Option A: Cl⁻  

The relevant half-reaction is:  

$\mathrm{Cl}_{2}+2e^{-}\to 2\mathrm{Cl}^{-},E^{\circ }=+1.36V.$  

The reduced form here is Cl⁻. Its corresponding oxidation (the reverse reaction) would have an electrode potential of  

$E_{\text{oxidation}}^{\circ }=-1.36V.$  

Option B: MnO₄⁻  

In the given half-reaction, MnO₄⁻ acts as the oxidizing agent (it is reduced to Mn²⁺). Therefore, MnO₄⁻ is not a good reducing agent.

Option C: Cr (metallic chromium)  

The relevant half-reaction is:  

$\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}+3e^{-}\to \mathrm{Cr},E^{\circ }=-0.74V.$  

Here, Cr is the reduced species. Reversing this reaction gives:  

$\mathrm{Cr}\to \mathrm{Cr}^{3+}+3e^{-},$  

with an effective oxidation potential of  

$E_{\text{oxidation}}^{\circ }=+0.74V.$

Option D: Mn²⁺  

In the MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ couple, Mn²⁺ is the reduced form. Its reverse (oxidation) potential would be:  

$E_{\text{oxidation}}^{\circ }=-1.51V.$  

When comparing the oxidation potentials (remember, a higher oxidation potential means the species is more willing to lose electrons), we have:

Cl⁻: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ }=-1.36V$  

Cr: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ }=+0.74V$  

Mn²⁺: $E_{\text{ox}}^{\circ }=-1.51V$  

Among these, metallic Cr stands out because its corresponding reduction half-reaction has the most negative potential ($-0.74V$). This negative value indicates that Cr (in its elemental form) is unstable relative to its oxidized form ($\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$) and, therefore, is the most eager to lose electrons. In other words, Cr is the strongest reducing agent.

Thus, the answer is:

Option C: $\mathrm{Cr}$

sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Direct bromination of aniline is fast and goes para (or to 2,4,6-tribromoaniline), so the para position must be blocked and the activation of $-\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$ moderated.

Aniline with $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{SO}{}_{4}$ forms anilinium hydrogen sulphate, which on heating at 453–473 K rearranges to sulphanilic acid (4-aminobenzenesulphonic acid); the $-\mathrm{SO}{}_{3}\mathrm{H}$ group now occupies the para position.

$\mathrm{Ac}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ acetylates the amino group to $-\mathrm{NHCOCH}{}_{3}$, a milder ortho/para director, so $\mathrm{Br}{}_{2}$ gives a single Br at the free position ortho to nitrogen: 4-acetamido-3-bromobenzenesulphonic acid.

Heating in water ($\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$, $\Delta$, acidic medium) reverses the sulphonation and removes $-\mathrm{SO}{}_{3}\mathrm{H}$; NaOH then hydrolyses the amide to free $-\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$, giving 2-bromoaniline.

(A) leaves the para position open and gives 4-bromoaniline; (D) has no step that removes $-\mathrm{SO}{}_{3}\mathrm{H}$, so its product keeps the sulphonic acid group; (C) brominates free aniline at 2, 4 and 6.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement (I) : The first ionization energy of Pb is greater than that of Sn .

Statement (II) : The first ionization energy of Ge is greater than that of Si .

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In group 14, the general trend is that ionization energy decreases down the group because atomic size increases.

Now check each statement carefully.

For Statement (I):

Pb and Sn belong to the same group.

Usually, ionization energy should decrease from Sn to Pb. But Pb shows slightly higher ionization energy than expected because of poor shielding by inner $d$ and $f$ electrons and relativistic effects. Due to this, the outer electrons of Pb are held more strongly.

So, the first ionization energy of Pb is slightly greater than that of Sn.

Statement (I) is true.

For Statement (II):

Ge lies below Si in group 14. As atomic size increases from Si to Ge, the outer electron becomes easier to remove.

Hence, the first ionization energy of Ge is less than that of Si.

So, Statement (II) is false.

Therefore, the correct option is:

$\text{Option D}$

Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift

$\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{I}_{2}(\mathrm{g})⇌2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})$

sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Starting from $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{I}{}_{2}$ only, the reaction $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{I}{}_{2}(\mathrm{g})2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})$ consumes $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{I}{}_{2}$, so their concentrations fall, while $[\mathrm{HI}]$ rises from zero.

At equilibrium the forward and backward rates become equal, so all three concentrations then remain constant and each curve becomes parallel to the time axis.

Graph (A) shows all three concentrations rising, graph (B) shows $[\mathrm{H}{}_{2}]$ rising and $[\mathrm{HI}]$ falling, and graph (D) shows $[\mathrm{I}{}_{2}]$ rising; only graph (C) shows both reactants decreasing and $\mathrm{HI}$ increasing from zero before all three level off.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement (I) : Experimentally determined oxygen-oxygen bond lengths in the $\mathrm{O}_{3}$ are found to be same and the bond length is greater than that of a $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$ (double bond) but less than that of a single $(\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O})$ bond.

Statement (II) : The strong lone pair-lone pair repulsion between oxygen atoms is solely responsible for the fact that the bond length in ozone is smaller than that of a double bond $(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O})$ but more than that of a single bond $(\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O})$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Ozone is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent structures, $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}$ and $\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$, so both O–O bonds are identical and have bond order 1.5.

A bond order of 1.5 lies between that of $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$ (2) and $\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}$ (1), so the O–O bond length in $\mathrm{O}{}_{3}$ (128 pm) is greater than that of $\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{O}$ (121 pm) and less than that of $\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{O}$ (148 pm). Statement I is true.

Statement II reverses this order (a bond cannot be shorter than a double bond and longer than a single bond at once), and the intermediate bond length is caused by resonance, not by lone pair–lone pair repulsion. Statement II is false.

Hence, the correct option is (C).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift

text: When Ethane-1,2-diamine is added progressively to an aqueous solution of Nickel (II) chloride, the sequence of colour change observed will be:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Aqueous nickel(II) chloride contains the green ion $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{6}]{}^{2+}$. Ethane-1,2-diamine (en) is a bidentate ligand, so each mole of en added replaces two water molecules.

$[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{6}]{}^{2+}+\mathrm{en}\longrightarrow [\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{4}(\mathrm{en})]{}^{2+}+2\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

$[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{4}(\mathrm{en})]{}^{2+}+\mathrm{en}\longrightarrow [\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{2}(\mathrm{en}){}_{2}]{}^{2+}+2\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

$[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{2}(\mathrm{en}){}_{2}]{}^{2+}+\mathrm{en}\longrightarrow [\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{en}){}_{3}]{}^{2+}+2\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$

The four species $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{6}]{}^{2+}$, $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{4}(\mathrm{en})]{}^{2+}$, $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}){}_{2}(\mathrm{en}){}_{2}]{}^{2+}$ and $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{en}){}_{3}]{}^{2+}$ are green, pale blue, blue/purple and violet respectively.

Since en is a stronger-field ligand than $\mathrm{H}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}$, each replacement raises $\Delta _{o}$, the absorbed light moves to shorter wavelength and the observed colour shifts from green through blue to violet.

Hence, the correct option is (C).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift

text: Consider a complex reaction taking place in three steps with rate constants $\mathrm{k}_{1},\mathrm{k}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{k}_{3}$ respectively. The overall rate constant $k$ is given by the expression $k=\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}k_{3}}{k_{2}}}$. If the activation energies of the three steps are 60, 30 and $10\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ respectively, then the overall energy of activation in $\mathrm{kJ}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ is $_________ . ($Nearest integer)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the overall energy of activation for the given complex reaction with rate constants $k_{1}$, $k_{2}$, and $k_{3}$, we start with the expression for the overall rate constant $k$:

$k=\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}k_{3}}{k_{2}}}$

The rate constant can also be expressed in terms of the Arrhenius equation:

$A\cdot e^{-E_{a}/RT}=\sqrt{\frac{A_{1}e^{-Ea1/RT}\cdot A_{3}e^{-Ea3/RT}}{A_{2}e^{-Ea2/RT}}}$

By comparing the exponential terms from both sides, we have:

$\frac{E_{a}}{RT}=\frac{1}{2}\left (\frac{E_{a1}}{RT}+\frac{E_{a3}}{RT}-\frac{E_{a2}}{RT}\right )$

This simplifies to:

$E_{a}=\frac{E_{a1}+E_{a3}-E_{a2}}{2}$

Substituting the given activation energies—$E_{a_{1}}=60\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, $E_{a_{2}}=30\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, and $E_{a_{3}}=10\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$:

$E_{a}=\frac{60+10-30}{2}=\frac{40}{2}=20\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

Therefore, the overall energy of activation is 20 kJ/mol.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift

text: The hydrocarbon $(\mathrm{X})$ with molar mass $80\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ and $90%$ carbon has $_______$ degree of unsaturation.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Mass of carbon $=\frac{80\times 90}{100}=72\mathrm{gm}$

Number of C-atoms $=\frac{72}{12}=6$

Mass of hydrogen $=\frac{80\times 10}{100}=8\mathrm{gm}$

Number of H -atoms $=\frac{8}{1}=8$

So molecular formula $\mathrm{C}_{6}\mathrm{H}_{8}$

D.U. $=6+1-8/2=7-4=3$

text: The observed and normal molar masses of compound $\mathrm{MX}_{2}$ are 65.6 and 164 respectively. The percent degree of ionisation of $\mathrm{MX}_{2}$ is $__________$%. (Nearest integer)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To calculate the percent degree of ionization of the compound $\mathrm{MX}_{2}$, we begin by considering its dissociation process:

$\mathrm{MX}_{2}\to \mathrm{M}^{+2}+2\mathrm{X}^{-}$

Next, we use the van't Hoff factor (i), calculated as the ratio of the normal molar mass to the observed molar mass:

$i=\frac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{observed molar mass}}=\frac{164}{65.6}$

Now, expressing the relationship of ionization in terms of the van't Hoff factor, we have:

$1+(3-1)α=\frac{164}{65.6}$

Simplifying this equation gives us:

$2α=\frac{164}{65.6}-1=\frac{98.4}{65.6}$

Solving for $α$:

$α=0.75$

Therefore, the percent dissociation, or the percent degree of ionization, is:

$\text{Percent dissociation}=75%$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift

text: The possible number of stereoisomers for 5-phenylpent-4-en-2-ol is $________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
5-Phenylpent-4-en-2-ol is $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OH})-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}$.


[IMG]

C2 carries four different groups ($\mathrm{H}$, $\mathrm{OH}$, $\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CHC}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}$), so it is the only chiral centre: R or S.

The C4=C5 double bond has two different groups on each carbon ($\mathrm{H}$ and $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OH})\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}$ on C4; $\mathrm{H}$ and $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}$ on C5), so it shows geometrical isomerism: E or Z.

The two stereogenic units marked * (one chiral centre and one stereogenic double bond) are independent, so the number of stereoisomers $=2\times 2=4$ (E-R, E-S, Z-R and Z-S).

Hence, the answer is 4.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 24th January Evening Shift
